extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students (or newcomers) learning how to write mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for writing clear, correct direct proofs and related proof techniques (vacuous/trivial proofs, inequalities, parity arguments), including definition style, logical flow, and presentation conventions for undergraduate-level mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof start/end markers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is customary to tell the reader 'the proof starts here' and 'the proof finishes there' — typically start a proof by writing 'Proof:' and finish it with a little square '□' (or ♦, ♢, ■).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an explicit 'Proof:' label at the start and a QED marker (square, filled square, diamond) at the end so readers can identify the proof block. Online versions may enclose the proof in a box and still end with the square.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbering definitions/results
rubrics_metrics.description: Number definitions, theorems, lemmas, corollaries, facts, etc., so they can be referred to easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign numbers to important items to permit cross-referencing. (Note: numbering schemes for equations are debated; number equations as appropriate for reference.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Make definitions easy to find and highlight them
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare definitions with 'Definition:' and avoid hiding important definitions inside ordinary paragraphs; highlight the defined term (inverted commas, italics, bold, underline) so the reader can find it easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place important definitions clearly and visibly; for key terms use typographic emphasis. Don't bury definitions in mid-paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'if' in definitions implies 'if and only if' (convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: In definitions the word 'if' is commonly used where 'if and only if' is really meant; this is conventional in mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers may safely assume 'if' within a definition is bi-conditional; however, be aware and explicit if ambiguity might arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of a good definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A good definition starts by defining objects and symbols involved, then states the main property, and follows up with additional related properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the pattern: (1) introduce objects/symbols, (2) define the property, (3) list related remarks/terminology and quantifier conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise with quantifiers and strictness in inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use explicit language for inequalities and quantifiers (e.g., 'strictly greater than one' vs 'greater than or equal to one') to avoid confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing in words, say 'strictly less than' for < and 'less than or equal to' for ⩽. Be explicit about existence ('for some') vs universality ('for all').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use distinct symbols for different instances
rubrics_metrics.description: When invoking definitions on multiple expressions, use different placeholder symbols (e.g., use k and ℓ) to avoid accidentally introducing unintended constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reusing the same dummy variable for different applications of a definition; doing so can inadvertently force equalities and produce incorrect conclusions (example: reusing k for n and n^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof structure: assume hypothesis and derive conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: In a direct proof, start by assuming the hypothesis is true and work through logically to the conclusion, often via intermediate statements (P1, P2, ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the chain of implications explicit: P ⇒ P1 ⇒ P2 ⇒ ... ⇒ Q, and use modus ponens to justify moving from one step to the next. Begin the write-up with the assumption and end with the derived conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate scratchwork (exploration) from final write-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof-writing breaks into two parts: scratchwork (exploration/strategy) where ideas are discovered, and the write-up, which is the polished, logically ordered presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scratchwork to find the approach but rearrange steps for correct logical flow in the write-up. Do not present the final proof in the order of exploratory manipulations if those started from the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct logical flow: start from known facts/axioms in the write-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the scratchwork began at the desired conclusion and worked backwards, the formal proof should start at known facts, axioms, or hypotheses and proceed forward to the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inequalities and other results, reorganize the argument so that each step flows logically from previously established facts rather than seeming to assume the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain vacuous and trivial proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: If an implication is vacuously true (hypothesis always false) or trivially true (conclusion always true), explain why — state that the hypothesis is false or the conclusion is always true and justify briefly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though no 'work' is required, explicitly note the reason so the reader understands why the implication holds and why it's useless for modus ponens or similar inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust level of detail to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a certain background for the reader but add details when in doubt; explicitly state facts you depend on if they might not be known to your audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If uncertain what the reader knows, include more intermediate steps or reminders of basic facts (e.g., Fact 3.0.2). For advanced audiences you may omit elementary justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard connective phrases for readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'Hence', 'It follows that', 'So', 'This implies that', and 'We can now write' make proofs more legible and help the flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these standard transitions to guide readers through the logical steps without verbosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name results appropriately (theorem/lemma/corollary/proposition/result)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Theorem' for important results, 'Lemma' for helper results, 'Corollary' for immediate consequences, and 'Proposition' or 'Result' for intermediate material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick names that reflect intended use and importance; lemmas are stepping stones, corollaries are immediate consequences, theorems are main results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful handling of inequalities when multiplying/dividing
rubrics_metrics.description: When you multiply or divide an inequality by a quantity, consider the sign—multiplying or dividing by a negative number flips inequality direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit facts (e.g., Fact 3.3.2) about signs; ensure denominators are non-zero; isolate terms (e.g., write x(x−3)) to avoid invalid subtractions of inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques: rewrite expressions to known nonnegative forms (e.g., squares)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common technique for inequalities is to rearrange to the square of an expression (e.g., (x−y)^2 ⩾ 0) or other known nonnegative quantities to derive desired bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scratchwork it is natural to start from the target inequality and factor; in the write-up start from the known nonnegativity and expand to reach the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity proofs: represent integers as 2k or 2k+1
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove statements about even/odd integers use the definitions n = 2k (even) or n = 2ℓ + 1 (odd) and manipulate algebraically to show the required form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state representations, keep dummy variables distinct, and show the resulting integer coefficient exists to conclude parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof by counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To show an implication is false, find a specific instance where the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false; one counterexample suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate the particular value (e.g., n=3) and check both hypothesis and conclusion to show the implication fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for hidden invalid steps and common faulty moves
rubrics_metrics.description: Review proofs for hidden invalid operations (e.g., dividing by zero, cancelling factors that might be zero, reuse of variable names that impose extra constraints) that invalidate arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyses of faulty proofs, identify where steps implicitly assume something (like x−y ≠ 0) or reuse the same symbol for different roles; remedy by adding cases or excluding problematic values explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful when manipulating expressions involving existence quantifiers ('for some')
rubrics_metrics.description: When definitions use existential language ('for some integer k'), treat that existence carefully in subsequent manipulations and explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you assert 'there exists k' and later produce a transformed expression, show how to exhibit an integer ℓ (in terms of k) to satisfy the required existential claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation economy: omit trivial algebra but ensure logical justification
rubrics_metrics.description: You may omit obvious arithmetic or basic associative/commutative facts but should not skip steps that hide logical leaps; aim for clarity without unnecessary verbosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prove basic field axioms each time, but supply enough justification so a reader with the assumed background can follow each implication in the chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: When constructing proofs of multiple cases, check all cases and indicate switching where needed
rubrics_metrics.description: For proofs that involve case-splitting (e.g., parity/combinations), ensure each case is addressed, and tell the reader how to switch symbols or arguments between symmetric cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proof treats 'assume x is odd and y even (otherwise switch x and y)', explicitly note that symmetry covers the alternate case, and verify no case is omitted.
